body:
What is air defence?

Air defence refers to the measures used to detect, identify, monitor and respond to threats arriving through the air. Depending on the system, threats may include aircraft, helicopters, unmanned aerial vehicles, cruise missiles and some ballistic missiles.

Missile defence is a related but more specific concept. It concerns protection against missiles. Not every air-defence system is designed to intercept ballistic missiles, and not every system capable of engaging aircraft can perform the same task.

Radar and other sensors

Radar stands for Radio Detection and Ranging. It uses radio waves to detect objects and obtain information about them. In a basic radar system, transmitted radio waves encounter an object and part of the energy returns towards the receiver. Processing the received signal can provide information such as the object's presence, distance and motion.

Radar is an example of an active sensor because it transmits energy as part of its observation process. Other systems use different forms of sensing.

  • Surveillance radar: Provides information about objects present in a monitored region.
  • Tracking radar: Provides repeated observations useful for following the movement of detected objects.
  • Electro-optical sensors: Use information from the visible or nearby parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.
  • Infrared sensors: Detect infrared radiation associated with objects and their surroundings.
  • Airborne early warning and control systems: Carry surveillance and command-related equipment on aircraft, extending the range of perspectives from which the air situation can be observed.

Each sensor has its own capabilities and limitations. No single sensing method can be assumed to provide complete information in every environment.

Command and control: turning observations into decisions

Command and control (C2) means the arrangements through which authorised personnel and systems receive information, assess a situation, coordinate available resources and direct an appropriate response.

In air defence, radar and other sensors provide observations. A command-and-control system helps combine and interpret this information. Decisions about a response are then made under the applicable military authority and procedures.

An interceptor is a defensive missile or other system used to engage an incoming threat. The interceptor is different from the radar that detects the threat and from the command-and-control arrangements that coordinate the response.

Why air defence is layered

A layered air-defence system combines different defensive capabilities because aerial threats vary in their characteristics. Short-, medium- and long-range defensive systems may perform complementary roles, while different sensors and command arrangements support the overall defence network.

Layering does not mean that every weapon can engage every threat. A system optimised for aircraft or drones is not automatically a ballistic missile interceptor. Similarly, the presence of several layers does not guarantee that every incoming object will be intercepted.

Ballistic missile defence

Ballistic Missile Defence (BMD) focuses on detecting and intercepting ballistic missiles or their re-entry vehicles. Broadly, interceptions may be described as:

  • Exo-atmospheric: Occurring outside Earth's atmosphere.
  • Endo-atmospheric: Occurring within the atmosphere.

These terms describe where an interception occurs. They do not themselves identify a particular Indian missile or prove that a complete national defence shield is operational.

On 10 and 11 June 2026, DRDO conducted flight tests demonstrating multi-layered ballistic missile defence capability. The announcement was published on 13 June 2026. The tests are evidence of demonstrated technological capability; they do not establish guaranteed nationwide protection against all possible missile threats.

Integrated Air Defence Weapon System

On 23 August 2025, DRDO carried out maiden tests of an Integrated Air Defence Weapon System (IADWS). The official announcement identified 3 kinds of defensive components:

  • QRSAM: Quick Reaction Surface-to-Air Missiles.
  • VSHORADS: Very Short-Range Air Defence System missiles.
  • Directed Energy Weapon: A high-power laser-based defensive system.

The system also included a centralised command-and-control arrangement. Its significance lies in the integration of different kinds of defence equipment rather than the use of one missile type alone.

Why saturation presents a challenge

Saturation refers broadly to a situation in which a defensive system must cope with many threats during a limited period. Air-defence systems have finite sensing, processing and response resources. The presence of multiple simultaneous threats can therefore increase the burden on detection, identification, decision-making and response.

Other general challenges include distinguishing relevant objects from background observations, coordinating several defensive systems, avoiding mistaken identification and maintaining reliable communications. The outcome depends on many circumstances; it should never be inferred from the number of available missiles alone.

Important distinction: A successful interception during a controlled trial establishes that specified test objectives were met. It does not establish perfect performance in every operational situation.

Prelims focus

  • Radar uses radio waves for detection and ranging.
  • Command and control connects observations with authorised defensive decisions.
  • An interceptor is a defensive engagement system, not a synonym for radar.
  • Endo-atmospheric and exo-atmospheric describe interception environments.
  • IADWS was tested on 23 August 2025 using QRSAM, VSHORADS and laser-based directed energy technology.
  • Trap: Multi-layered defence does not imply guaranteed interception of every threat.

[Sources: DRDO, 'Missiles and Strategic Systems', command, control, guidance and testing functions, consulted 14 November 2026; Ministry of Defence, Press Information Bureau, 'DRDO successfully conducts maiden flight-tests of Integrated Air Defence Weapon System', 24 August 2025; 'DRDO demonstrates the nation's next-gen defence capabilities', 13 June 2026; 'DRDO Successfully Completes User Evaluation Trials of Akash-NG', 23 December 2025.]

title: Air and Missile Defence: Radar, Sensors, Command and Control, Interceptors and Layered Protection

body:
Why missiles are discussed in international security

Missile technology has important implications for national defence, deterrence, international security and the spread of military capabilities. The same broad areas of technology, including propulsion, navigation and guidance, may also have peaceful applications in aerospace and related fields.

Deterrence means seeking to discourage a hostile action by creating an expectation of unacceptable consequences or by reducing the likelihood that the action will achieve its purpose. Arms control refers to agreements or arrangements intended to regulate particular military capabilities or behaviour. Non-proliferation seeks to limit the spread of specified weapons or associated technologies.

These concepts are related but not identical. A country may pursue deterrence while also participating in transparency or export-control arrangements.

Missile Technology Control Regime

The Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR) is a voluntary arrangement through which participating governments coordinate export controls concerning missiles, unmanned delivery systems and related technology.

India became an MTCR member on 27 June 2016.

A frequently cited MTCR Category I benchmark is a complete rocket or unmanned aerial vehicle delivery system capable of a range of 300 km or more while carrying a payload of 500 kg or more. The 2 conditions are considered together for this benchmark.

This threshold is an export-control classification criterion. It is not a universal rule prohibiting MTCR members from possessing, developing or testing missiles beyond 300 km. The MTCR is also not the same as a nuclear-arms-reduction treaty.

MTCR examination distinction: 300 km and 500 kg are associated with a particular controlled delivery-system category. They do not define every missile, every export-control item or the maximum missile range permitted to India.

Hague Code of Conduct

The Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation (HCoC) is a voluntary, legally non-binding international transparency and confidence-building arrangement concerned with ballistic missile proliferation.

India joined the HCoC on 2 June 2016. The arrangement includes measures such as annual declarations and prelaunch notifications concerning ballistic missiles and space launches.

The HCoC differs from the MTCR. The HCoC emphasises transparency and confidence-building; the MTCR coordinates export controls. Neither should be described as an organisation that directly operates India's missile systems.

How to interpret defence-development announcements

Reports about missile development use terms that indicate different stages. Understanding these terms is as important as remembering the names and dates.

  • Development flight test: A trial intended to evaluate specified technical or flight objectives.
  • Maiden flight test: The first reported flight test of a particular system or version.
  • User evaluation trial: Testing or evaluation involving intended users to assess whether a system meets relevant requirements.
  • Production or procurement: Activities associated with manufacturing or acquiring equipment; they do not automatically establish operational deployment.
  • Induction: The process by which a system is formally brought into service with the relevant military organisation.

The precise administrative steps differ among projects. The central rule is that testing, evaluation, production and induction are not interchangeable words.

Verified selected developments

The following table records major publicly announced Indian missile and air-defence developments relevant to this lesson. Its information cutoff is 14 November 2026. Status descriptions refer to what the cited official announcement established, not to an assumed later change.

Date of eventSystem or programmeWhat was officially reported
18 April 2024ITCMSuccessful flight test using indigenous propulsion.
16 July 2025Akash PrimeSuccessful high-altitude production-model trial.
23 August 2025IADWSSuccessful maiden tests of integrated defensive components.
23 December 2025Akash-NGUser evaluation trials successfully completed.
27 February 2026VSHORADS3 successful user-validation flight trials.

23 July 2026KushaSuccessful maiden flight test.

Connecting the whole topic

Missiles can be understood by asking several independent questions. What is their intended role? This distinguishes Akash, Astra, Nag and other categories. How do they travel? This distinguishes ballistic, cruise and quasi-ballistic missiles. How do they move and navigate? This separates propulsion, navigation, guidance and seekers. How are aerial threats detected and handled? This explains sensors, command and control, interceptors and layered defence.

Indian programmes provide concrete examples of these concepts. IGMDP establishes the historical foundation; later programmes show continued development of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, air-to-air weapons and air-defence systems. International arrangements such as the MTCR and HCoC add the wider security and regulatory context.

Prelims focus

  • India joined the MTCR on 27 June 2016.
  • India joined the HCoC on 2 June 2016.
  • The MTCR Category I delivery-system benchmark combines 300 km range and 500 kg payload.
  • HCoC is voluntary and legally non-binding.
  • As of the 14 November 2026 cutoff, the 5 November Pralay announcement reported user evaluation and imminent induction, not completed induction.
  • Trap: A missile's classification, development milestone and operational status answer different questions.

[Sources: NCERT, Contemporary World Politics, Class 12, Chapter 7 'Security in the Contemporary World'; Ministry of External Affairs, Annual Report 2016–17, 'Disarmament and International Security Affairs', MTCR and HCoC membership; Ministry of External Affairs, 'Disarmament and International Security Affairs Overview', export controls and HCoC transparency measures, consulted 14 November 2026; Missile Technology Control Regime, Technical Annex, Category I, Item 1.A, 3 November 2023; Ministry of Defence, Press Information Bureau, 'Indigenous Technology Cruise Missile successfully flight-tested', 18 April 2024; 'Successful trial of Akash Prime at High-Altitude', 17 July 2025; 'DRDO successfully conducts maiden flight-tests of Integrated Air Defence Weapon System', 24 August 2025; 'DRDO Successfully Completes User Evaluation Trials of Akash-NG', 23 December 2025; 'DRDO conducts successful flight-trials of Very Short-Range Air Defence System', 27 February 2026; 'India conducts successful flight-trial of Advanced Agni missile with Multiple Independently Targeted Re-Entry Vehicle system', 9 May 2026; 'DRDO demonstrates the nation's next-gen defence capabilities', 13 June 2026; 'DRDO conducts successful flight-test of Long Range Land Attack Cruise Missile', 15 June 2026; 'DRDO conducts successful maiden flight-test of Kusha Long-Range Surface-to-Air Missile', 23 July 2026; 'Agni-4 Ballistic Missile successfully test-fired', 6 August 2026; 'DRDO conducts successful flight-test of quasi-ballistic missile Pralay', 5 November 2026. Online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]
